{{Short description|Mathematical technique in general relativity}}
'''Fermi–Walker transport''' is a process in [[general relativity]] used to define a [[coordinate system]] or [[Frame of reference|reference frame]] such that all [[curvature]] in the frame is due to the presence of mass/energy density and not due to arbitrary spin or rotation of the frame. It was discovered by Fermi in 1921 and rediscovered by Walker in 1932.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bini |first1=Donato |last2=Jantzen |first2=Robert T. |year=2002<!--Not 2003--> |title=Circular Holonomy, Clock Effects and Gravitoelectromagnetism: Still Going Around in Circles After All These Years |url=https://www.sif.it/riviste/sif/ncb/econtents/2002/117/09-11/article/21 |journal=Nuovo Cimento B |volume=117 |issue=9–11 |pages=983–1008 |arxiv=gr-qc/0202085 |bibcode=2002NCimB.117..983B |archive-date=2023-12-14 |access-date=2023-12-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231214035101/https://www.sif.it/riviste/sif/ncb/econtents/2002/117/09-11/article/21 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Fermi–Walker differentiation==

In the theory of [[Lorentzian manifold]]s, Fermi–Walker differentiation is a generalization of [[covariant differentiation]]. In general relativity, Fermi–Walker derivatives of the [[spacelike vector|spacelike]] vector fields in a frame field, taken with respect to the [[timelike vector|timelike]] unit vector field in the frame field, are used to define non-inertial and non-rotating frames, by stipulating that the Fermi–Walker derivatives should vanish. In the special case of [[inertial frame]]s, the Fermi–Walker derivatives reduce to covariant derivatives.

With a <math>(-+++)</math> sign convention, this is defined for a vector field ''X'' along a curve <math>\gamma(s)</math>:

:<math>\frac{D_F X}{d s}=\frac{DX}{d s} - \left(X,\frac{DV}{d s}\right) V + (X,V)\frac{DV}{d s},</math>

where {{math|''V''}} is four-velocity, {{math|''D''}} is the covariant derivative, and <math>( \cdot , \cdot )</math> is the scalar product. If

:<math>\frac{D_F X}{d s}=0,</math> 

then the vector field {{math|''X''}} is Fermi–Walker transported along the curve.<ref>{{harvnb|Hawking|Ellis|1973|p=80}}</ref> Vectors perpendicular to the space of [[four-velocity|four-velocities]] in [[Minkowski spacetime]], e.g., polarization vectors, under Fermi–Walker transport experience [[Thomas precession]].

Using the Fermi derivative, the [[Bargmann–Michel–Telegdi equation]]<ref>{{harvnb|Bargmann|Michel|Telegdi|1959}}</ref> for spin precession of electron in an external electromagnetic field can be written as follows:

:<math>\frac{D_Fa^{\tau}}{ds} =  2\mu (F^{\tau \lambda} - u^{\tau} u_{\sigma} F^{\sigma \lambda})a_{\lambda},</math>

where <math>a^{\tau}</math> and <math>\mu</math> are polarization four-vector and [[magnetic moment]], <math>u^{\tau}</math> is four-velocity of electron, <math>a^{\tau}a_{\tau} = -u^{\tau}u_{\tau} = -1</math>, <math>u^{\tau} a_{\tau}=0</math>, and <math>F^{\tau \sigma}</math> is the [[Electromagnetic tensor|electromagnetic field strength tensor]]. The right side describes [[Larmor precession]].

==Co-moving coordinate systems==
{{main|Proper reference frame (flat spacetime)#Comoving tetrads}}
A coordinate system co-moving with a particle can be defined. If we take the unit vector <math> v^{\mu} </math> as defining an axis in the co-moving coordinate system, then any system transforming with proper time is said to be undergoing Fermi–Walker transport.<ref>{{harvnb|Misner|Thorne|Wheeler|1973|p=170}}</ref>

==Generalised Fermi–Walker differentiation==

Fermi–Walker differentiation can be extended for any <math>V</math> where <math>(V,V)\ne0</math> (that is, not a [[Spacetime|light-like]] vector). This is defined for a vector field <math>X</math> along a curve <math>\gamma(s)</math>:

:<math>\frac{\mathcal D X}{d s}=\frac{D X}{d s} 
+ \left(X,\frac{DV}{d s}\right)\frac{V}{(V,V)}
- \frac{(X,V)}{(V,V)}\frac{DV}{d s}
- \left(V,\frac{DV}{d s}\right)\frac{(X,V)}{(V,V)^2} V ,</math><ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=astro-ph/0411595 |title=Geometry of Dynamical Systems|date=2004 |last1=Kocharyan |first1=A. A. }}</ref>

Except for the last term, which is new, and basically caused by the possibility that <math>(V, V)</math> is not constant, it can be derived by taking the previous equation, and dividing each <math>V^2</math> by <math>(V,V)</math>.  

If <math>(V,V)=-1</math>, then we recover the Fermi–Walker differentiation:  

<math>\left(V,\frac{DV}{d s}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{ds}(V,V)=0\ , </math> and <math>\frac{\mathcal{D} X}{d s}=\frac{D_F X}{d s} .</math>
